analysis.one_liner: Makes police force against protesters a federal civil rights violation and removes the death penalty for such cases.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with three House Democrats, has sat without any action in the House Judiciary Committee since late May 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes an existing federal criminal civil rights law that already makes it a crime for government officials, including police, to violate someone's federally protected rights. It would spell out that using force while responding to a protest counts as such a violation, so officers who injure or kill protesters could face federal charges under this statute. At the same time, it removes the death penalty as a possible sentence when such a violation causes death.
analysis.who_benefits: People who attend protests, and anyone concerned about police accountability, gain a clearer federal tool for charging officers who use force against demonstrators. Defendants facing charges under this law also benefit from the removal of the death penalty as a possible sentence.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the federal criminal civil rights statute (18 U.S.C. 242), which prohibits government officials from depriving people of federally protected rights, to specify that use of force during a response to a protest constitutes such a deprivation [S2].

This clarification makes it explicit that officers who injure or kill people while responding to a protest can be charged under this federal criminal statute, which prosecutors have historically used unevenly against law enforcement [S2].
The bill removes the death penalty as a sentencing option when the violation results in death or when aggravating factors are present [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers and the agencies that defend them would bear greater exposure to federal criminal charges for force used during protest responses. Federal prosecutors and courts would handle additional cases. Some may see a cost in removing the death penalty from the statute's most serious cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement officers facing federal charges

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the death penalty as a penalty option when a rights violation results in death, which critics could argue weakens the maximum consequence for the most serious cases [S2].

Expanding the statute to cover force 'during a response to a protest' could be criticized as vague: officers facing violent or dangerous situations at demonstrations would face greater criminal exposure, which a good-faith opponent could argue deters effective policing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main value is symbolic and clarifying: the underlying conduct is already unlawful under federal law, so its practical effect depends on how prosecutors use the clarified statute. Removing the death penalty is a genuine trade-off that cuts both ways — it spares defendants the harshest punishment while arguably reducing the maximum deterrent. Because the bill has seen no committee action, none of these effects has been tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and nothing has happened to it since — no hearing, no vote, and no sign of movement.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 29, 2025, joined by Reps. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi and Pramila Jayapal [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and that referral is the last action in the bill's history [S5].
The bill has two cosponsors, both House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and agencies are better off because the bill has not advanced: the clarified federal criminal exposure for force used against protesters has not been enacted. The status quo on protest policing remains unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement, since the bill went nowhere

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to clarify that police force against protesters violates the federal criminal civil rights statute

for.name: Reps. Bennie Thompson and Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's two cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; with Republicans holding 223 of 435 House seats and controlling the House agenda, a bill with only Democratic sponsorship faces long odds.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill would expose officers to clearer federal criminal liability for force used during protest responses, but it also removes the death penalty from the statute's most serious cases, softening the maximum punishment. Police unions generally oppose expanded criminal liability for officers, which runs against protesters' interests in accountability.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the House Judiciary Committee with only a handful of cosponsors and no majority-party support rarely receive a hearing or a vote; the most likely path is that the bill sits in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
